hops.afterHeading: Where: every fibre reports one patch of the world
hops.title: Why Siamese cats go cross-eyed
hops.text: Siamese cats are famous for their crossed eyes, and the story starts at the optic chiasm. Siamese cats carry a pigment-related genetic variant, and some of their temporal-retina fibres cross at the chiasm when they should stay on the same side. In their 1971 paper, Hubel and Wiesel found that each hemisphere's cortex also mapped a 20 degree strip of the same-side visual field, fed entirely by the opposite eye. White tigers have two copies of a recessive variant that reduces coat pigmentation; the white tiger brain examined in 1973 had a disrupted thalamic layer consistent with similar misrouting, though that tiger's eyes were normally aligned.

sources.citation: Hubel DH & Wiesel TN, 'Aberrant visual projections in the Siamese cat', J. Physiol. 218(1):33-62 (1971).
Guillery RW & Kaas JH, 'Genetic abnormality of the visual pathways in a "white" tiger', Science 180(4092):1287-1289 (1973).
Xu X et al., 'The genetic basis of white tigers', Curr. Biol. 23(11):1031-1035 (2013).

image.caption: In Hubel and Wiesel's Siamese cats, misrouted fibres gave each hemisphere a strip of the same-side visual field.

hops.afterHeading: Why a bar beats a spot
hops.title: The glass slide whose edge woke up a cortical cell
hops.text: In 1958, in a windowless basement room at Johns Hopkins, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel held one cat cortical neuron on their electrode for nine hours. For three or four hours they got nowhere with spots and black dots glued onto glass slides. Then, while inserting one of those slides into the slot of their ophthalmoscope, the cell went off over the audio monitor like a machine gun. The dot had nothing to do with it. As the slide went in, its edge cast a faint, sharp shadow on the retina, a straight dark line, and the cell wanted that line at one narrow range of angles.

sources.citation: Hubel DH, Nobel Lecture, 'Evolution of Ideas on the Primary Visual Cortex, 1955-1978: A Biased Historical Account', 8 December 1981.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A hand sliding a glass slide with a small black dot into a vintage optical instrument next to an old loudspeaker on a lab bench.
image.caption: The black dot did nothing; the straight shadow cast by the slide's edge made the cortical cell fire.

hops.afterHeading: The map: retinotopy, magnification and columns
hops.title: Inverting goggles do not flip the map in visual cortex
hops.text: A popular claim holds that if you wear upside-down goggles long enough, your brain flips the world right side up again. In 1999, David Linden and colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Frankfurt tested it on four people who wore inverting prisms and mirror spectacles for six to ten days. Their movements adapted quickly. None of them reported the world turning upright. Functional MRI in three of them found no alteration in the retinotopic map of early visual cortex. The volunteers learned to act in a flipped world while V1 kept its map as it was.

sources.citation: Linden DE, Kallenbach U, Heinecke A, Singer W & Goebel R, 'The myth of upright vision. A psychophysical and functional imaging study of adaptation to inverting spectacles', Perception 28(4):469-481 (1999).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pair of prism goggles on a cafe table showing an upside-down view of a coffee mug and pastry through the lenses.
image.caption: After days in inverting goggles, movement adapted while early visual cortex kept its map unflipped.
